utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I meanwhile use the time to address an issue, and it will end with a question mark, and there will be no time at this moment for the parties to respond but perhaps to start thinking about it. It is about the reopening of the Prosecution's case. The Chamber is due to deliver decisions on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that there is no translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no translation. Is there translation now? Still there isn't, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Somehow it's on the fifth channel this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the fifth channel this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Usually it's on the sixth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which then raises the issue where we find the French, because the French transcript has also to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I say we do this but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is a problem with the French channel. There is no interpretation into French because none of their microphones can be switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Their microphone is on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we check whether it has now -- on channel [Previous translation continues] ... nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It works for the French booth now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On channel 6 there is B/C/S, and 5 is still no French yet. Yes. I was informed that the French channel is now functioning as well. Then we can proceed. Witness, you may be a bit surprised but we had a technical problem with the interpretation which has been resolved but that was the reason -- I do understand that the witness now doesn't receive -- okay. Could the usher assist so that the volume will be ... Witness, can you now hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the technical problems, having been resolved, there is no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- time to address the issue which I wished to address. Let's first continue. Witness, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. MacDonald will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31882, and I'd ask this document not be broadcast, Your Honours. If we can turn to page 3 in the B/C/S and page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, this is a statement of a Muslim in Siprage given in the year 2000. I'd like to draw your attention to the B/C/S six lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And in page 5 in the English, seven lines from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: A sentence beginning: "After the weapons had been surrendered ..." And the author states: "After the weapons had been surrendered, the SDS and VRS authorities began to arrest the population on a large scale" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where exactly are you reading from, Mr. MacDonald?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Actually, in the English, there is some kind of yellow background --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And to continue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot understand the witness at all. He's not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak into the microphone. And could the usher assist in adjusting the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Let me just find the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that it's rather to the bottom of the page. Have you found it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The author states: "After the weapons had been surrendered, the SDS and VRS authorities began to arrest the population on a large scale and to take them away to camps. At the beginning, prominent and wealthy Bosniaks were taken to the camp, but later on they went down the line. Thus it was on 7 June 1993 I was arrested and taken to prison in Kotor Varos." Mr. Ubiparip, around the time you became commander of the 1st Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, did you know about these arrests taking place in Siprage?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in the B/C/S but stay on the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to skip a few lines and take you to the paragraph beginning, "after my arrest ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The author continues: "After my arrest, another delegation visited Siprage, headed by a VRS general, Momir Talic who, at the time, as far as I can remember, held the post of commander of the Krajina Corps of the VRS." The author is correct that Momir Talic was commander of the 1st Krajina Corps in June of 1993; isn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The author continues: "In addition to Talic, other officers and local SDS ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we can turn the page in the English, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: "... representatives were in the delegation." Mr. Ubiparip, were you part of this delegation that went to Siprage in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: But either as commander of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade or as Chief of Staff of the 22nd Brigade, you must have been aware of General Talic heading this delegation visiting Siprage?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember at all that General Talic ever came to Siprage while I was brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Reading on, the author continues: "Again, the delegation members addressed the residents of Siprage in their already established manner. After the meeting, a large-scale expulsion of Bosniaks from Siprage ensued. The Bosniaks of Siprage were expelled in organised convoys while their property was seized and distributed to Serbian residents." Were you aware of an organised expulsion of Bosniaks from the village of Siprage in June 1993 or shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1993, there were no expulsions from the moment when I became commander. Before that, I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When you moved your command post to Siprage, were you aware that the village was quite empty of its inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Siprage with my command, for purely military reasons this was a planned relocation. The entire population of Siprage was autochthonous, that's what we called them. And they were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 02559k.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the census in 1991 taken in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I believe we only need the B/C/S of this, Your Honours. If we can turn to the second page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, this excerpt, Mr. Ubiparip, deals with the Kotor Varos municipality. I'm looking for the --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The third name from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So if we scroll down --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Siprage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: -- you see Siprage, yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: These numbers deal with earlier decades, but if you look along to your right, you'll see that it's number 40, and that corresponds to Siprage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, please, and look for number 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just at the bottom there next to number 40, we see there are 952 people in total.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And then thereafter, the numbers are 1 Croat, 745 Muslims, and 188 Serbs in 1991. If I can just ask you to recall that number, 745 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if the Prosecution can now have 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The document you're about to see, Mr. Ubiparip, is an Official Note from the state security centre in Banja Luka on the 2nd of May, 1994. I'd like to take you to the start of the second paragraph, beginning: "Having established ..." Now, the second paragraph records how many Muslims are working in Kotor Varos municipality. We have 25 in the Vrbanja DD, 15 in the Drvo-prevada DD, 5 in the sawmill, 4 in the Siprage ZZ, and about 150 in labour brigades. The note continues that this number includes all able-bodied men and that they are under the control of the VRS. From your experience of being commander of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, the only VRS military unit on the territory at this time, it's true that in May 1994 there were up --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It's true that there were approximately 200 or less able-bodied Muslim men working in Kotor Varos municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And there is only four able-bodied men working in Siprage -- Muslim men, my apologies, at this time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, I'd seek to tender 65 ter 02559k, that is the census excerpt, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam -- yes, Madam Registrar, the census excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 02559k receives Exhibit number P7106, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. And then this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 31964 receives Exhibit number P7107, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution now have 65 ter number 31965. Again, I'd ask this document not be broadcast, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ubiparip, the document you're about to see is another Official Note recorded by the state security department in Banja Luka. It is again dated the 2nd of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd look to move to page 2 in both languages to start. Your Honours, I do plan to deal with the first page but in private session for reasons I hope that will become apparent, but I'll deal with the second page in open session just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ubiparip, this document discusses people that the BH government has requested be captured or, if not possible, liquidated, and we'll come to that part in a moment, but if I can take you to the last paragraph, this note states: "These people have not been randomly selected, they participated in the illegal disarming of Muslims in Siprage, the collection of legal weapons, and had been told to explain to the Muslim population that it was necessary to respect and be loyal to the Republika Srpska organs of authority in order to avoid unwanted incidents, in which they have so far been successful." It's true, isn't it, that the Muslims in Siprage --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the Muslims in Siprage were illegally disarmed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That happened before I came. Mr. Mujko Zuhric explained things to me. He said there was a planned action and it had a positive effect on the security situation in that territory. When I became commander, or once I became commander, there was no illegal disarmament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if at this point we can move into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, I'd like to move to a different topic now, the topic of the village of Garici. You're aware of the village of Garici in Kotor Varos municipality; aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And it swore loyalty to Republika Srpska and surrendered its weapons at the outbreak of the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, the Defence has led evidence that this village remained untouched throughout the war. But that's not accurate, is it, Mr. Ubiparip?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, as I said yesterday, that Muslim Major Asim Aganbegovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said? The interpreters had difficulties in understanding you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. From the said village, I had one of my officers, a Muslim, Asim Aganbegovic. He was loyal to the local authorities, and he informed me that there were no problems and that the people of Garici continued to live normally, and I had occasion to see that for myself. They even had a successful business that continued to work, a chicken farm, rather well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if we can move into private session briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, I'd like to move to another topic and that is events in Vecici village in November 1992. Now, I am aware that you were still Chief of Staff of the 22nd Brigade at this point, but you knew that Vecici village continued to resist the VRS up until November 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And you were aware at the time that Muslims had tried to break out of Vecici on 3rd November 1992.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that they intended to do that, but on the 4th or the 5th, I saw that a part of their forces had broken through to Mount Vlasic, and only later did I learn it was an effect of their intention. I mean, those people who wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31970.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, this is a report signed by you -- or typed-signed, my apologies, by you on the 3rd of November, 1992. It's being sent to the commands of the 1st Krajina Corps and the 30th KRD. Do you see, sir, that it is type-signed by you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can I take you to point 4, which states the: "Focus is on the protection of manpower power and MTS and accommodation facilities from Muslim OGs, which have left the village of Vecici near Kotor Varos." So it was reported to you on 3rd November 1992 Muslims had left the village of Vecici; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Who reported that to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the person who reported it to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, on the 4th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In fact, can the Prosecution -- well, I'd move to tender this document first, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31970 receives Exhibit P7110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P00441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, could you tell us how much time you'd still need? Because you're at the hour you estimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Only a couple of minutes for this topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Couple of minutes. That's accepted. Let's then finish soon and then take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ubiparip, this is a report from the 4th of November, 1992 from the 1st Krajina Corps to the VRS Main Staff. It's dated -- ah, I said that already. And they are reporting under the second point in the second paragraph that there has been a massacre -- a brutal massacre of Green Berets. Now, sir, on the 4th of November, 1992, did you get this information and pass it on to the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was basically received by Mr. Janko Trivic, and then he made me aware of it. Since I was linked through the chain of command through the command of the 22nd Brigade, of course I was aware of this. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: My final question, Mr. Ubiparip: Who reported it to Janko Trivic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know. I don't know. I arrived in his command post later, where he informed me about the situation that had to do with that which had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you before we take the break. In your statement you say that you had prisoners of war in the operations you took part in. Now, here we see a report which refers to 200 men being captured. Do you know whether they were also registered as prisoners of war and that their names and lists would be submitted to the Red Cross, as you describe it, for prisoners of war in any operations you took part in, in paragraph 20 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Three combatants from the Muslim army who were captured by my forces during combat. I took these men. And then on the basis of the Geneva Convention, I registered them with the Red Cross, I provided them with first aid until they were taken over, and I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you registered three prisoners of war during the whole of your career in -- and never anyone else was taken prisoner, also not civilians which were detained or nothing happened? Thank you. Yes, the witness didn't answer, but I should have put on the record that you, by nodding your head, that you agreed that it was only three, but could you please put that clearly on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. I personally, yes. In combat operations, my unit took them prisoner. We processed them. And -- how do I put this? On the basis of Geneva Convention that we all had, we sent them further on. The Red Cross then took care of them until their matter was completely resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you had the Geneva Convention, you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had a text of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Each and every one of my soldiers had that text, how to behave in war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Defence tell the Chamber how much time they would need after the break, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it's going to be up to 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would urge the parties to see whether it would be possible to conclude the testimony of the next witness today. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ubiparip, at one moment you were asked by the Prosecution about the report concerning what you did in relation to the coming of units from Vecici. This is my question: Can you tell us to the best of your recollection what was the information that you actually received from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the superior command, I did not receive this information. Rather, it was from Commander Trivic who was commander of the Celinac Brigade. The breakthrough of that unit took place in his area of responsibility. So I just happened to be there. And then through official channels, I informed my brigade command and, naturally, the corps as well about that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, Mr. Trivic, was he also commander of the Operations Group Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Peulic was commander then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at that time P7710. P7710 [as interpreted]. I shall repeat because I think it hasn't been recorded again -- properly again, it is 7110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's have a look because the previous number, Madam Registrar informed me that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He has changed it now. It's now correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have now a new number. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on paragraph 4 of this regular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this report you, Mr. Ubiparip, are informing the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, and in the upper right-hand corner it also says the 30th KRD.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 30th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what this is?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this report in paragraph 4, you say: "Focus is on the protection of manpower and MTS and accommodation facilities from Muslim" DGs, "which have left the S Vecici near Kotor Varos." Please tell us what does this mean, Muslim DG?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are groups for breakthroughs; that is to say, they broke through, up there, and then for their own protection, we put them up until a final solution was to be found; physically protected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those moments you, your unit, did you have any combat clashes with this sabotage group that had left the village of Vecici?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing I wish to ask you in relation to the answers you provided during cross-examination. During the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm a little bit confused by the way you put this -- the last question to the witness. In the document in the English translation, we see "accommodation facilities from Muslim OGs." In -- what you read was "DG." Could you please clarify what you mean by that? Is that a mistake or is it a mistranslation? And especially the witness didn't explain what these letters stand for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that you have before you the B/C/S, so then I'd like to ask the witness about this. Could we zoom in on that part in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "The Muslim," is it D or is it O?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So paragraph 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, now after the number 4, in the third or fourth line, I believe, there is this abbreviation. Is it DG or OG?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: DG.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question: What would DG mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we defined it as sabotage groups of Muslim units that had broken out of Vecici in the direction of Vlasic. And over there, they surrendered to us. So we took them over and we protected them -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the question was what the letters DG stand for. No long explanation. Just these two letters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Diverzantska Grupa," "sabotage groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will finish with the question that I started with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ubiparip, during these years of war, would it have been lawful and legitimate for anyone, irrespective of ethnic background, anyone who is not involved in the military could have military weapons?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is paramilitary organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question. During wartime and during imminent threat of war, was every military-age man subjected to conscription or work obligation?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P7107, could we please take a look at that document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to see this document during cross-examination. Sir, on the basis of your experience during those years of war, a military conscript, would he rather join the army and go to the front line or take work obligation?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they preferred work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What would be the reason why people would prefer work obligation to military obligation at the front line?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the primary reason is physical and biological protection of their life, number one. Number two, it is easier to get the basic material resources that one needs for themselves personally and for their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this document now. In the second paragraph, it says -- and you were asked about that, about the involvement of Muslims in work, and there is a reference to the Siprage co-operative, and there were four persons that were involved in that, according to this report. Do you have any knowledge about this co-operative Siprage? On the 2nd of May, 1994, was it working then; and how many people did it employ?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: These four that appear, I see the others here, too. I knew them in a way. From the very beginning, they were permanently employed in that co-operative, you see. So the number of our, should we call them Serb citizens, were involved, first of all, in the Army of Republika Srpska was only natural that - how do I put this? - through work obligation, the needs of these companies were met so that they could achieve their programme objectives and tasks for which they existed in the first place. Let me say straight away that many of these Muslims wanted to go and fight against their own, as it were, but I would not allow that because I wanted to prevent a fratricidal war that had a very negative effect on our people during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But please, if you can, if you have such knowledge, in 1994 how many people worked in this co-operative, this farming co-operative in Siprage?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN UBIPARIP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally cannot remember the number, but it all depended on the needs involved. It was around this level. But let me tell you one more thing: All workers, all citizens, if I can put it that way, in that area were involved in the same food process that I had organised. We were all eating from the same pot, as it were. So there was no negative effect in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, thank you for your answers and thank you on behalf of the Defence team was General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Nothing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further. Then, Witness, I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague, and I would also thank you for having answered all the questions that were put to you, Mr. Ubiparip, and put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are calling Mr. Nikolic, Vinko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I would ask that I be excused from the Court please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are excused, Mr. MacDonald. Is it Mr. Zec who will cross-examine the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. I would simply note, as we indicated to Mr. Lukic before the beginning of this court session, that Mr. Nikolic was advised of his rights pursuant to Rule 90(E) at the beginning of his testimony in Karadzic case. So in light of the questions I anticipate to ask him today, it may be more advice -- to advise him of his rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then do that right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have a question for you. All the references to adjudicated facts and to parts of the schedule of the indictment, how do we have to understand those?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a table of concordance, Your Honour. It's under 1D5324. So we'll probably -- we will offer that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we are supposed to look at that prior to the witness coming to court, or ... was it announced somewhere that we would be presented a table?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would -- have it on my list that it's one of the documents I should offer as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we may say a little bit more about it. Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, before the Defence will start its examination, I'd like to inform you about Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I'll read it to you. It says: "A witness," and that, in this case, would be you. "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question, and testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." So if you have concerns whether answers, truthful answers to questions would possibly incriminate you, please address me. You'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just need help from the usher. I have to distribute statement summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To the booth. Now, Mr. Lukic, I'll make one brief observation. Of course the Judges, having read the 92 ter statement, are supposed to have read the statement of the witness before he comes to court in order to fully understand the testimony. If you do not provide us in advance with such tables, we are lost. How could we possibly understand the evidence not knowing what these adjudicated facts are about? Do we have to find and compare the cases? That's really not what we expect you to do. So please provide next time always well in advance any table, and I must say that even it would have been better to, also for purposes of relevance, to have a statement which is focused on this case rather than on another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you said the document -- the list of concordance would be on the list of exhibits or documents to be used with the witness? In my list, I don't find any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just checking, Your Honours, when it was sent. I have to ask my Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would like to hear that from you. But we are taking our task very serious, Mr. Lukic, and it's in your hands whether we can perform that task. And it's in your own interest that we seriously perform our task. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you tell us slowly your full name.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My name is Vinko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens 1D2519, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- did you give a statement to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see on the screens the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to review this statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has the statement accurately recorded what you said to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, what is stated in this statement, is it truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would you answer the same way as when you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this moment we would offer the statement of Mr. Nikolic, 1D2519, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D02519 receives Exhibit number D892, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, still I don't have any news regarding this table of concordance, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we're waiting for a question or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for your approval to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Well, usually if I do not stop you, as you know -- it's on the screen now, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this table of concordance into the evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we first verify. It is a two-page document. Have you verified that they are, because we couldn't do that, that they are literally the same in Karadzic and in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that in other case when they were not the same, we redacted statement of the previous witness. So I suppose that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have you verified that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My Case Manager did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. There are no objections, so therefore, Madam Registrar, the number would be, but we will carefully consider whether or not they are literally the same. Mr. Zec, any observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Only to note that this is first time that we see this list, so we are not in position to offer any comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was informed several days ago that it was composed, and I suppose that it was sent as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good tradition that those responsible verify whether what they are reported, whether that is accurate, yes or not. But for the time being, we'll admit it into evidence. But if there is any -- if there is any difference between the language of the Karadzic and the Mladic statements, we'll revisit the issue of admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we clarify, is this the only page or is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- a second page? Can we have a look on the second page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there is one comment on the second page about adjudicated facts modified by the Chamber and a text which apparently refers to a footnote, a footnote which appears in relation to Mladic adjudicated fact number 1146. Now, which of the two now appears then for 1146, Mr. Lukic? Is it the Mladic adjudicated fact? And if so, does that have any effect on the comment given by the witness on that adjudicated fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously adjudicated facts in this statement are all from Karadzic trial, because it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how do I have to understand footnote 1 in relation to 1146 where, on page 2 of this statement, we read: "Adjudicated facts modified by the Chamber ..." And then it says -- no, no. "Added text, houses were looted, and people fleeing were deprived of the valuables that they were carrying with them." Now, which Chamber -- is that a change made by the Mladic Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then -- I take it, then, the witness did not comment on the whole of the text in the Mladic adjudicated fact. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I have another question. In paragraph 34 of the statement, there is a reference to adjudicated fact 2523 in the Karadzic case. This is not contained in the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are trying to contact our Case Manager. He's not responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- I have to state that the list of concordance is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that he -- I was just informed that this list was sent on the 27th of January to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: By e-mail or uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By e-mail. And it was uploaded into e-court as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say it was also sent by e-mail?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the information I just got, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I also am looking at Mladic adjudicated fact number 1146. Am I mistaken that 1146 was not adopted as an adjudicated fact by this Trial Chamber? I'm just trying to check that very quickly. But on the list I am consulting at this moment, 1146 is empty. But that can, perhaps, be verified. The list will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D05324 receives D893, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will not have any questions for this witness. I will just read short statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Vinko Nikolic was a member of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most municipality. He will testify on the role and nature of Sanski Most Crisis Staff. Vinko Nikolic will testify about the causes of the conflict between Serbs and Muslims in Sanski Most. The witness will explain that there was no plan to expel Muslims or Croats from the municipality. He will testify about the presence of paramilitaries in his municipality. He will explain the role of SOS group in Sanski Most and their relationship with the authorities. Mr. Vinko Nikolic will testify that there are lots of examples where Muslims continued to work in the municipality; in the land registry or as school teachers. From 1992 to 1995, more than 8.000 Muslims continued to live in Sanski Most municipality. The Sanski Most Crisis Staff issued an order that all property was to be looked after and temporarily allocated as needed to Serbian refugees. And that's the end of the statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness, could we have the statement of the witness, which is now P892, on our screens -- no, D892 on our screens. And could we go to most likely page 7 in the English, paragraph 25. Yes. And in the -- yes, that's also. We have the right page in B/C/S as well. Witness, there I read. The question was to "list the prisons, prisoner of war camps, and collection centres in your municipality." Your answer was: "I have listed the investigation centres. There were no prisons or camps in Sanski Most." Now, did you list those investigation centres and did you give it to the Defence that interviewed you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did list those investigation centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You gave it to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that when the statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when my statement was taken for Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when did you for the first time meet with the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in March or April 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were interviewed then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And no -- did you say exactly the same as you said when you were interviewed by the Karadzic Defence or were there details which were different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you interviewed or did you just go through the statement you'd given to the Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then spontaneously you -- were exactly the same questions put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They put questions to me about things they needed answered, and I answered these questions, just as I did when I was making the previous statement for Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the questions were not exactly the same, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the questions were identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you also give a list of the investigation centres to the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I told them about investigation centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they ask for a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a written list. I just answered the question which investigation centres existed in Sanski Most. At that time, I was in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you then give us that list now, which investigation centres there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I was in Sanski Most in April and May, there were three investigation centres at that time: One was at the public security station; the second was in the company called Betonirka, about 100 metres from the public security station; and the third one was in the Hasan Kikic Primary School, about 200 metres from the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put something on the record. The Chamber was just informed that the list of concordance -- or the document which is now D893, MFI, was sent to the Prosecution and the Chamber ten minutes ago at 11.30 by the Case Manager of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we'll not, in the presence of the witness, further discuss what happens here. But if you present a question and an answer, that the witness says he lists the investigation centres without naming them, and then to expect this Chamber to be able to evaluate the mere observation of a witness that he has listed them, without knowing else what is on that list. But, happily enough, he now has corrected this. Mr. Zec, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Zec. Mr. Zec is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And simply to note that we also received the same e-mail as His Honour Judge Fluegge just mentioned on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll not qualify -- I'll not speak aloud what is on the my mind at this moment as the appropriateness of this way of proceeding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that you were a member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, and you also say that you were member of the SOS, the Serbian Defence Forces. So simply to clarify: You were a member of the Crisis Staff from its creation on 14 April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you were the SOS representative on that Crisis Staff; yes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P3294.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is the diary of Nedjelko Rasula. He was the president of the Crisis Staff. You have seen this diary before, and I'll simply ask you for one clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if we can have page 19 of the English, page 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: As it can be seen on the bottom of the English page, and it's in the middle of the page in the B/C/S to the right, these are notes of the 14th April 1992 session of the SDS Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if we can move to the next page in the English. Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And there is a list of the Crisis Staff members; that's item 4. Last name in the list is Zvonko Nikolic. Now, this is reference to you, Vinko Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a misspelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. At a later meeting on 30th May, 1992, you were appointed Crisis Staff member in charge of vehicles; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: On 18 June 1992, you were appointed as a commissioner for transport; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw that later because I spent a whole month on the front line in the corridor and we returned only in the end of June, so I did not attend these meetings of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31963.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you will see, it's a decision reached by the Crisis Staff at its meeting on 18 June 1992. It says: "Vinko Nikolic is appointed transport commissioner ..." So this is your appointment decision to the commission for transport; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31963 receives Exhibit number P7111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I would like now to focus to the SOS unit. Is it correct that the SOS carried out many tasks and activities in Sanski Most municipality, some of the tasks were transporting and disseminating weaponry, capture of the municipality building, mopping up operations, participating in the operations at the corridor; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Partly. As for arming, our members could not have armed the Serb people because we did not have any weapons. The other facts are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, can I just get a clarification from the witness. Sir, you're saying you did not have weapons. How, then, did you participate in the operations in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not have any weapons before the conflict broke out in Sanski Most. While the conflict was breaking out, we were a Territorial Defence unit of Sanski Most, and it is only then that we received weapons. That was the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once you received weapons, did you distribute them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was personal weapons of each and every one of our members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. Once you then received weapons, did you distribute them? Or disseminate them, if I may use the word used by Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We distributed them only to our own members, the members of our own unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we will discuss arming a little bit later. But can we have now the 65 ter 31386.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a report on the activities and the participation in combat of the SOS as per the plan of the 6th Krajina Brigade. Within a few first lines of that text, it explains that the SOS was formed and placed under the command of the 6th Brigade. And then it states: "All actions to date have been carried out with the approval of the Brigade Command. Since the establishment of the 6th Krajina Brigade, the members of the SOS have carried out many important tasks and activities as the members of the Sanski Most SDS." And there is a list of the tasks and activities. So these were, Mr. Nikolic, some of the SOS activities carried out in co-ordination with the 6th Krajina Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As for arming and the distribution of weapons, that was carried out by people who were in the 6th Sana Brigade and who were at the front line. When they would come to Sanski Most on leave, then they would bring weapons that they had captured in combat, and then they would give these weapons to the members of their own households, to their parents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we'll talk about -- later about arming. But for the rest of these tasks, you confirm that's more or less what you were doing; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, our soldiers took part in the front line. That was people who joined us later, because the 6th Sana Brigade had come from the Croatian front, and about 20 men who had experience came into our unit, and that is why they were -- or rather, that is because they had been at the Croatian front. The taking of the municipal building is correct as well. We took part in Mahala, Vrhpolje, and Hrustovo. Combat operations in Bihac. Some individuals of ours took part in that day, Vitovlje-Babanovac, our entire unit was attached to the battalion of the 6th Sana Brigade. I don't remember exactly which battalion this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the SOS activities were reported to the Crisis Staff. That's also correct; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. This was -- well, because of this propaganda, huge propaganda against the SOS in Sanski Most. While we were at the front line, we decided to send them a letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zec, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you leave this document for a moment, my basic question is very simple: The SOS activities --

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- they were reported to the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff provided financial support to the SOS members; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Only in the period of April and May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31867, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a record of the Crisis Staff meeting held on 16 June 1992. Focusing on item 4, it says: "Anicic submitted a report on the work of the military police and the activities of Njunja's sabotage platoon." Item 4: "Crisis Staff approved the financial assistance (and rewards for the sabotage platoon and military police) ..." Now, Mr. Nikolic, commander of the SOS was Dusan Saovic, also known as Njunja; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So Njunja sabotage platoon in this document is the SOS unit. That's clear here?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Anicic, that's Colonel Nedjeljko Anicic, commander of the Serbian TO; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 65 ter 31386 and 31867 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 31386 receives Exhibit number P7112. Document 31867 receives Exhibit number P7113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7112 and P7113 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that it's time for break. If you want to break now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break now. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Nikolic, and we'd like to see you back quarter past 12.00. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we take the break, we saw the table of concordance that was about adjudicated facts. What about items in the indictment? Is there a similar table? Because references are made to the annexes to the indictment. And I take it that since that statement was taken by the Karadzic Defence, that its reference is to annexes in the Karadzic indictment. But if I'm wrong, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are definitely not wrong, Your Honour. I will check during the break what's -- do we have the same chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can tell you already that at least the first one mentioned Appendix A to the indictment that the number referred to doesn't exist in ours, as far as I could see. It took me only one minute to verify. We take a break and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, I could briefly deal with a matter I started with this morning, which is the following. The Chamber is due, as I said, to render decisions on four motions related to the proposed expert witnesses and one Rule 92 bis motion, all related to the Prosecution's reopening of its case. Nonetheless, the Chamber wants to have a preliminary discussion with the parties about scheduling. As the Chamber held previously, it prefers that all the evidence for the reopening is presented en bloc. The Chamber suggests that the reopening evidence be heard in May or June of this year, and the Chamber wonders whether that timing would create any problems for the parties. If you could immediately respond by "yes" or "no," of course we would hear that. But if you want to think about it or perhaps even discuss it among the parties, then, of course, the Chamber would hear your response at a later moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we were talking about the activities of the SOS before the break. It is correct, is it, that the SOS worked closely with the Crisis Staff in the implementation of the instructions from the republic level SDS and the ARK level SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen 65 ter 06364.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is another of the documents that you saw before. And this is a report on the work and activities of the SOS acting as a intervention platoon with the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can see last page of the document first. Focusing on the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the signatures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, could we have B/C/S left-hand side and English at the right-hand side. No, it's -- apparently is difficult. We started with B/C/S at both sides, then we had English at both sides, we are now back at B/C/S at both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will ask the witness for the signature, so maybe we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- only the B/C/S is relevant. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nikolic, the signatures that we see in the B/C/S version, these are signatures of Dusan Saovic, that's the first; in the middle, it's your signature; and the last signature, it's Goran Cankovic; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And so we are clear, so this report was prepared by the SOS members; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now have page 3 in both versions. In English, we will be looking at third paragraph, and in the B/C/S, very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It states: "Remember the meeting we had on the premises of the Serbian Orthodox church where we particularly warned about the slow implementation of the conclusions reached by the Bosnia-Herzegovina SDS and the Bosnian Krajina." So this is an example of your support and encouragement in the implementation of the instructions from the higher level; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We were talking previously about arming, and you said that the SOS was not armed until April 1992. In fact, the SOS helped arm the Serbian people in Sanski Most before the conflict broke out; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was not organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to page 2 of your report that we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Page 2 in both languages. In the middle of the page in English, towards the end of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you are here discussing how the SOS kept the peace from May 1991, and you say: "These young men, I'm thinking of the seven lads who tirelessly brought weapons from various warehouses and points and armed the Serbian people, risking that the weapons fall into the hands of Ustashas and Green Berets." So, Mr. Nikolic, this is a reflection of your activities related to arming of the Serbian people in Sanski Most before the conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I've already said that that had not been organised. Individuals that had the possibility of getting weapons armed their neighbours and family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Among other SOS activities was also blowing up buildings owned by Muslims and Croats and arresting SDA and HDZ leaders; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were arrests on [Realtime transcript read in error: "And"] orders from the Crisis Staff and the public police station during the months of April and May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just see. The transcript reads "there were arrests and orders." Could we verify whether there were arrests and orders or whether there were arrests that were ordered by the Crisis Staff? Is it that the arrests were ordered by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have page 2 of the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- and page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- we go to page 2, on this question of the SOS --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- arresting people. Sir, the penultimate paragraph in English, I don't know where it will be in the B/C/S, reads in the middle: "No one should take credit for the capture of SDA and HDZ leaders other than the SOS and in part the Serbian police for its action."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is page 3 of the B/C/S. Thank you, Mr. President -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any comment on that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we carried out the arrests, the members of the police and the SOS, because the police force was smaller then because the Muslims and Croats had left. So the Territorial Defence Crisis Staff ordered us to help bring in extremists, armed Muslims, and their representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the reality is the SOS was involved in blowing up the buildings and capture of non-Serb leaders in order to intimidate non-Serb population in Sanski Most. That was the reality; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the reality was that it was Serbian cafes that were first blown up in Sanski Most. Those were the first ones that were not exactly blown up but damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this Chamber has received some evidence about these incidents that you're just referring to. But my question was: You were involved in these activities to intimidate non-Serb population of Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, this was not done in an organised way. It was only individuals who could have done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is SOS report. You, SOS, did it; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Individuals from SOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The SOS tasks and activities also included taking over public institutions; for instance, even before the take-over, on 28th February, 1992, the SOS took over the SDK - that is, the public auditing service - by force and removed the Croat director; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Not by force, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have page 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When power was shared, the SDK came to the Serbs. And since the director didn't want to leave, a few of us went there to take the keys from her and hand the keys over to Mr. Rasula, and then it was their task to select a new head of the SDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Page 4 of the English, page 5 of the B/C/S of the SOS report that we have on the screen. Towards the end of the page in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It states: "We also" -- "We must also mention how we resolved a previous problem of the SDK." And it continues: "Despite Alija's police, they weren't Alija's police but that's how we called them, so you Serbs won't hold it against me. We fellow Serbs carried out a raid on the Sanski Most SDK, took away the keys from the stubborn Croatian woman director who refused any form of co-operation or agreement and continued according to plan." So, Mr. Nikolic, you took over the SDK by force; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say "attack" here. It says "barging in." That's different from an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this 65 ter 06364 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06364 receives Exhibit number P7114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7114 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You state in response to question 10 that after the liberation of the municipality building, there was a period of chaos during which the -- during which roads were blocked and telephone lines were down. So now irrespective of any problems with roads or telephone lines, the Sanski Most Crisis Staff continued to be in contact with the ARK and republic level authorities throughout this period; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say that individuals and groups used this period of chaos for their own benefits. And during this period, Mr. Nikolic, the SOS and the military police confiscated a number of vehicles and goods at check-points; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This was a confiscation of trucks of Agrokomerc that were moving from Kljuc towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So just that we are clear, you are talking about Agrokomerc trucks. And Agrokomerc, that was a food processing company based in the area of Velika Kladusa. So they were distributing food and you basically confiscated these trucks at the check-points. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These trucks went further towards Serbia, Hungary, I don't know. They were all stopped, and the goods from the trucks were distributed to the population, all three ethnic communities, and the Crisis Staff was in charge of the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So we are also clear, the Velika Kladusa area, that's what Serb authorities considered as Muslim territory; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: A total of 29 Agrokomerc trucks were confiscated and you were placed in charge of these trucks on behalf of the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At later meetings of the Crisis Staff, I was given this task to guard the trucks when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: On the orders of the Crisis Staff, you provided these vehicles to various entities and individuals, such as 6th Krajina Brigade, the military police, and the SOS unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Requests were sent to the Crisis Staff, and we decided who needed these vehicles and we gave these vehicles to those organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The SOS used a number of these vehicles, including one truck to which they fixed a semiautomatic gun on top; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, because SOS was an intervention platoon attached to the command of the Territorial Defence. They asked for a vehicle and they adjusted it to become a combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The SOS used this truck with the semiautomatic gun on top in mopping up operations in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At Vrhpolje and Hrustovo. And when the corridor was being broken through and when we lost it in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, could I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your whole line of questioning started by referring to what the witness said, at least that's what I take it in paragraph 11, that individuals and groups used this period of chaos for their own ends. And then you suggested that trucks were confiscated. The witness then explained how the Crisis Staff and the SOS was involved in the confiscation of those trucks. But when you refer to individuals and groups in paragraph 11 of your statement saying there was looting and burning of houses, some of the refugees driven from Muslim-controlled towns in BH came to Sanski Most to seek a roof over their heads, what individuals and groups did you have on your mind there, or would that include the SOS when confiscating trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the confiscation of trucks was carried out on orders from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was apparently, then, not an example of what you refer to as individuals and groups using this period of chaos for their own ends. Could you -- what group -- could you tell us about one group and what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
