utterances.text: [Interpretation] That night when the municipality was liberated, since the police and the SOS group were in the municipality all night, individuals, various groups of looters, started looting in town, cafes, the supermarket, and so on, and that only stopped when the 6th Sana arrived in town in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say various groups. And again, I'll repeat: Could you give us, for one such group, composition? What exactly did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were groups, ordinary groups of citizens that were looting, that were probably stealing food, because they had fled from Croatia. Perhaps some small groups of locals as well, because nobody was arrested that night so it couldn't be proven who they were, these people in these groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that they had fled from Croatia. Did you think that these were Serbs who did that or...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Serbs who had fled from Croatia who had come to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you can't tell us specific persons forming a group and what exactly that group did? Apart from that, no action --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Stores had been broken into, windows had been broken, and food, cigarettes, and alcohol were taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in order to control this chaos, as you say, the Crisis Staff was establishing check-points around the town and municipality; correct? That was one of the functions of the Crisis Staff, to order where a check-point can be established or set up; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The order of the Crisis Staff was to place check-points, but the chief of police and the police decided operationally where they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 28414.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these are conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff meeting held on 7 May 1992. Towards the end of the page in item 6, it provides that Crisis Staff appointed you in charge of the Agrokomerc trucks. And in item 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, we need e-court page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item 9 says: "The existing check-point at the gas station of Tomina shall be removed and a new one set up at the Vrhpolje bridge." So this is a reflection of the reality that Crisis Staff made decisions where to set up check-points in order to control the movement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The chief of the security station was also a member and it was his proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document to evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28414 receives Exhibit number P7115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7115 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Just to finish up with these Agrokomerc trucks, you said the SOS used them in mopping up operations, but also these trucks were used for transport of Muslims and Croats out of municipality to Manjaca and other places; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Only for Manjaca. Two trucks were requested from the public security station in order to transport Muslims to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Turning now to the issue of dismissals. You say in response to question 12 that all citizens of Sanski Most, regardless of their ethnicity, were allowed to remain in their jobs if they respected the constitution of Republika Srpska. And, in fact, Mr. Nikolic, this is not correct. We have already seen example of the forcible removal of the Croat director of the SDK before the war. After the Serb take-over, other non-Serbs were also removed from their posts in other municipal institutions, such as the health centre and the court. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know about the court and I know about the health centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you know about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that the director of Muslim ethnicity was supposed to be replaced and the directors of Serb ethnicity were supposed to be appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P2410, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we look at that -- Could you tell us then why they were to be replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Adil Aganovic was president of the court, and he was a prominent and extremist member of the SDA. And also the head of the health centre too. I can't remember his name. He was also a prominent member of the SDA, and his orientation was an extremist one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you can see that the orientation of a doctor, I take it he was a doctor, was an extremist one? Is it that he disagreed with the Serb power or was it -- what was it that made him such an extreme person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to the report of the organs that carried out the investigation - that was, the police of Sanski Most - they came to learn that he gave vast amounts of money for arming Muslim paramilitary organisations; whereas, the president of the court from the safe, he took all the money and gold and he put it in Mahala, a different facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that this is documented in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes. The police informed us about that. As for the police on-site investigation and the conclusions, I didn't see that. However, they just informed us that that is what had been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, such documents could perhaps be in favour of the Defence because they would explain that it was not on the basis of ethnicity that people were replaced but because there were serious allegations of abuse. So, therefore, the Chamber, if you could get hold of that material for the evaluation of the evidence, it would certainly assist far more than just sweeping statements. Even in this statement we see that the witness is telling us that a certain order from the Crisis Staff is where a specific category of prisoners are mentioned, that it's misinterpreted. But unfortunately, the statement doesn't say which document that is. And so that it's very difficult for us to find out whether it really is a misinterpretation or whether there is a claim for misinterpretation which is not supported by that document. I mean, the Chamber wants facts, to the extent possible documentary evidence, rather than sweeping statements. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. P2410 is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these are conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, 24 April, 1992. Item 8, end of the page, it says: "Mladen Lukic, Vinko, and Boro, tasked with preparing the appointment of the acting director of the Health Centre in Sanski Most." Vinko, this is you, yeah? That's a reference to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you already indicated that this was -- this position was held by a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And shortly after you filled this position with a Serb whose name was Bosko Grubisa; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have now 65 ter 06569.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These are conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff meeting, 29 April 1992. At the first conclusion, it says: "... changes to be made to all officials of the Municipal Court of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most be appointed as acting official (Vrkes, Vrucinic and Nikolic are in charge of this)." Again, you are here named as Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the fact is that all non-Serb judges were removed, including Judge Nedzad Muhic, Azra Alabegovic, and Adil Draganovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When their director was dismissed, they quit their positions on their own because our task was only to replace the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, these people they were detained in Sanski Most and subsequently transferred to other locations, such as Manjaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were locked up and transferred in July, I believe. I don't know. I think my unit was away at that time. I don't know the exact date when they were transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you the following. The document reads that all officials at the municipal court must be appointed. Was this then after they had quit it? Because you explained this by saying "we were only tasked by the president to be replaced." But had they quit it then already before the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is about all officials, not Muslim officials. We received an order to replace the president of the court and to replace him by a Serb. We gave that job to Radovan Stanic. After the appointment of Radovan Stanic, the other officials in the municipal court just quit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was he appointed, if you know, Radovan Stanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember the date. Perhaps two or three days after this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in the decision it says already that all officials must be appointed in the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most of the municipal court. It doesn't limit itself to the president. It suggests that it is just a replacement of all officials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only replaced the president of the court based on the evidence we had against him. The other officials included Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. They were not only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those Serbs who left the court, they were not then later appointed again or...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were reappointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the president of the court appointed his own judges. Because it's the president that makes appointments of the judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those are, as far as Serbs are concerned, the same as who had left the court before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They accepted to work in the court again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was any job offered to non-Serb judges or officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. That was the job of the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question. You said these three men Mr. Zec named, Mr. Muhic, Mr. Alabegovic, and Mr. Draganovic, they quit their positions on their own. Why were they locked up and transferred to Manjaca? What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've said already the police was in charge of detaining people, interrogating them, and sending them on to Manjaca for further processing. I mean the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said only the director, the head of the court, was dismissed, but the others left their job on their own will. Why then -- have you any idea why they were detained and transferred to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said, I was on the front line at that time, and I did not look into these documents of the Crisis Staff again. I don't know why each individual was transferred to Manjaca and other investigation camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And Judge Muhic, he suffocated to death en route to Manjaca camp as one of the people who you assisted in replacing with Serb judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was talking about the president of the court, not Muhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was about Mr. Muhic. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Muhic left or quit his position on his -- of his own will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you also said that judges were taken to Manjaca. The question now is whether you know that Judge Muhic was suffocated to death when he was being transported to Manjaca camp, whether that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about that from others because I was at the front line at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These people who suffocated to death on their transport to Manjaca, which you refer to in paragraph 23 of your statement, you say they died due to great heat and a lack of oxygen. Now, this happened because they were packed into trucks with no ventilation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these were the trucks that you provided; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Those were the trucks supplied by the Crisis Staff, and I forwarded them on the orders of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Turning now to a different topic. In response to question 28, you state that from mid-May all members of the SOS were placed under the command of the VRS. Now, during the mop-up operations in Sanski Most at the end of May/early June 1992, including Mahala, Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, during which the SOS participated, the unit was subordinated to the 6th Krajina Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were actions in the mopping up of Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You state in response to question 30 that the attack operations in Mahala and elsewhere were not planned in advance. This Chamber has received evidence, including the attack order and testimony of some of the Defence witnesses, explaining that the mop-up operation in Mahala and elsewhere were part of a planned and co-ordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This can be found in P2411 and transcript page 30736.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So it's not true, Mr. Nikolic, that these were spontaneous attacks. They were well planned and co-ordinated attack operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, every attack is preplanned, but it was not planned in advance in this case until Muslims started to return fire from individual parts of Mahala and threatened lives on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, can you invite the witness to explain the difference between "preplanned" and "planned in advance"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you heard His Honour, Judge Orie's question. Can you explain to us what is the difference? What do you mean by "preplanned" and "planned in advance"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, planning much in advance is what I meant, for an operation. Whereas, the action in Vrhpolje and Mahala was planned 6 to 12 hours before the beginning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say "planned in advance" is a longer period of time, whereas it may be "preplanned" and that could be a shorter period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immediate planning just before the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you one additional question when we are at paragraph 30. You commented on the adjudicated fact mainly by saying that it was not planned and it was all in response to provocations, but you did not comment on the attacks themselves; for example, Mahala, was there any shelling involved? Were any mortars fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was shelling in Mahala with M60 mortars, which belongs to infantry weapons; hand-held zolja, rocket launchers; and such. That was used in the action in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you give us a few specific targets that were attacked by the weaponry you'd just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That kind of weapon is used against targets from which you see fire by the enemy against troops that are advancing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you say that kind of weapon is used. Were they used in that way; for example, in Mahala? Were you targeting troops in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, where were these troops in Mahala? Were they in the streets, on the markets, in the houses? Where could they be found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of them were in fortified houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there a lot of damage to those houses in Mahala when you used rocket launchers, mortars, hand-held zolja - that's rocket launchers, yes? Was there a lot of damage to those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the houses that were hit by such grenades and rockets were damaged, but they were not destroyed. It was not the kind of damage that could not be repaired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many of the houses in Mahala, for example, were damaged? Was it one house or was it ten houses or was it every one out of four? Could you give us an impression as to what ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak about my unit. The axis of our action was towards the left bank of the Sana River, and I believe we targeted four or five houses. I cannot speak about other units, because I was not present on the other side of the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this was Mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mahala is the centre of town, densely populated, with four or five streets along the whole length of the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say, "I cannot speak about other units, because I was not present at the other side of the action," do you mean other Serb units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, other units involved in that operation. Alongside us there were members of the 6th Sana Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you gain the impression that their attack was less fierce than yours in terms of the use of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, the resistance was less in that part of the neighbourhood than in the part that we covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I was asking about, rather, the use of weaponry by those who attacked Mahala. The other units you spoke about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's also infantry weapons. Zolja and Osa launchers and hand-held launchers, artillery, could not be used there because there was only the Sana River between Mahala and the other part of town. If artillery had been used, it would have been easy to overshoot and hit the other part of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was no risk when you used mortars, or do you consider mortars not to be artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A 60-millimetre mortar is an infantry weapon. Infantrymen carry those mortars themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I go back to my question, whether the use of weaponry in the attack was any less or less fierce in the units that were next to you or at the other side of the town, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean you don't know or was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Larger calibre weapons were not used, otherwise we would have heard the detonations of a large-calibre weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the intensity of the weapons that were used, that's what I'm trying to find out, whether that was similar to your unit or whether it was different in those other units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said we didn't use that kind of weapon so much there because the resistance in that part of the neighbourhood was less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you did fire zoljas and you did fire mortars -- mortar shells, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every intervention unit has these as part of their arsenal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking whether it was part of their arsenal but whether you used it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I personally use it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said we used it in four or five cases against features from which fire was opened at us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, these operations in Mahala, the goal of the Mahala and the target of these operations in Mahala were civilians. People, the citizens of Mahala, after the operation were detained in the sports hall in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: 24 hours before the attack, public announcements were made on the radio appealing to Muslims from that area to surrender their weapons. However, women, children, and the elderly left of their own accord and we put them up in the sports hall. Of course, not all of them left. There were certainly civilians who said. So after the combat was over, we moved those civilians to the stadium in Krkojevci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the place name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the name of the place that you said in your last sentence for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Football stadium in Krkojevci. It's a neighbouring village to Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence that in this attack on Mahala, that this attack resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians and that no significant amount of weapons were found. So these people were attacked, they were captured, they were prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I refer Your Honours to P2889.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were captured and moved to another location pending the restoration of normal conditions in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, did you want to make break now or I can continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I don't have that much. Maybe ten minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes' time. Also looking at you, Mr. Lukic, would you then prefer --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will finish this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you then prefer to take the break now, or would you rather use the time for the break after the whole cross-examination has been concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whatever Your Honours deem fit. I don't have any preferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, the advantage of continuing is that you are going to the time of the break. So unless there's strong opposition against it, then we would like you to finish your cross-examination now and take a break in approximately ten minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In response to question 12, you say that more than 8.000 Muslims continued to live in Sanski Most municipality. In reality, less than half of that number - 3.350 - remained in Sanski Most in 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am talking about Muslims and Croats. I said about 8.000. A census was not carried out in the villages where the majority population is. Muslims did remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your statement, you say 8.000 Muslims and not Muslims and Croats. There only referring to Muslims, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why then -- how I do have to understand your last answer, "I am talking about Muslims and Croats. I said about 8.000." Why then including Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they also lived in the area of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, again, not true, because by 1995 in Sanski Most were 1.050 Croats. If I add these Muslims that I mentioned, 3.350, it adds to 4.400 people. So, again, not correct that there were 8.000 Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most in 1995. It was half of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know whose estimate that is, since there was no census at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I then ask you: How do you know that there were 8.000? How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Free estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's your own estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my very own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you tell the Karadzic Defence that in 1995 that it was your estimate that 8.000 Muslims continued to live there, or did you give that as a number as some kind of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just told them on the basis of their question how many Muslims there were in Sanski Most during the war, and my answer to them was about 8.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said on the basis of their question. Was there any suggestion in the question that it would be 8.000, or did you come up spontaneously with that number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I spontaneously came up with that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So now according to the 1991 census, there were over 30.000 Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most municipality. By February 1995, the Banja Luka State Security Service estimated there were a bit over 4.400 Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is P3853.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So it is not true, Mr. Nikolic, that there were more than 8.000 Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most. In fact, only, like, a fraction of it, like 4.000, left in Sanski Most in 1995. That's the reality, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, that question has been asked, that question has been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That question has been answered and the witness explained that the 8.000 he mentioned was just a rough estimate on his part. Therefore, there is no need to further explore that matter, unless there are new aspects which you want to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you repeatedly talk about the voluntary nature of the departure of Muslims and Croats from Sanski Most. In response to question 17, you say they requested and decided to leave, and the authorities had an obligation to help them. In response to question 24, you say the civilian authorities, the police, and the army, did not plan, instigate, or order the permanent removal of Muslims from Sanski Most. The reality is, Mr. Nikolic, the Serbian authorities wanted Sanski Most to be a Serbian town, and they held the view that the most efficient solution was to transfer Muslims and Croats from Sanski Most to Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the meetings of the Crisis Staff that I attended, there was no mention of the mass movement out of the other two ethnic communities. Another matter are the wishes of certain officials, but I'm not going into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let me quickly show you two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: 65 ter 06462. These are minutes of the 9th Session of the Sanski Most Executive Committee. At page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: There is a discussion about -- item 4. There is a discussion about how many Muslims and Croats left the municipality and how many wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see next page in both languages. Towards the top of the English page. And in the B/C/S, this is in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Vlado Vrkes, SDS municipal president, said: "We have to persist in this work because this is what the soldiers and the people of Sanski Most require us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we see the top of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "We have to persist in this work because this is what the soldiers and the people of Sanski Most require of us because this has to be a Serbian town. Also said, Manjaca cannot take anymore."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now see one more document. It's MFI P7015.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is the SDS bulletin Informator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We need page -- English page 30 and B/C/S page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And here we see conclusions of the SDS Municipal Board meeting on 24 June 1992. Item number 2, it says: "The most efficient and the most peaceful solution on national strife is the transfer of people from one area to another. In that sense, some Muslims and Croats should be relocated from Sanski Most to Central Bosnia ..." So this is a reflection of the reality, Mr. Nikolic. The Serbian authorities wanted Sanski Most to be a Serbian town, which was achieved through various matters, one of which was transfer of Muslims and Croats from Sanski Most to Central Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time I was not a member of the SDS, and I was not a member of the Executive Board, and I was not a member of any administration in that kind of responsibility. These are conclusions that were reached while I was at the front line. I cannot give my comments on what Vlado Vrkes, Rasula, and the rest of them think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 65 ter 06462, and I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06462 receives Exhibit number P7116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, before we take that break -- you were -- Mr. Zec, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. I just got note that frankly document 062 -- 065 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Zec please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That the document under 65 ter 06569 is not admitted and I would ask that it be admitted into evidence, if I failed to do that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06569 receives Exhibit number P7117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Before we take the break, Witness, could I ask you the following. You answered whether a portion of a document was read to you: "At that time I was not a member of the SDS, I was not a member of the Executive Board, and I was not a member of any administration in that kind of responsibility. These are conclusions that were reached when I was at the front line ..." And you cannot give your comments on Vlado Vrkes, Rasula, and the rest of them. However, in your statement, paragraph 24, when you were asked about whether authorities at the local municipal level supported or instigated or -- well, a lot of other versions of what you could do with the permanent removal, you said: "I said earlier on that the political leadership tried to protect all citizens of Sanski Most." Now, which of the two is it? That you say I don't know what they said, or I wasn't there and therefore I cannot tell us [sic]; or is your answer that these people, indeed, were only aiming to protect everyone rather than to support, plan, instigate -- well, the removal of others? Which of the two we should take most seriously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just spoke about the time during which I was on the Crisis Staff, and at these sessions there was no mention of any permanent removal of the other two peoples. I can testify about those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you say -- your answer was given purely on the basis of what you personally experienced when attending the Crisis Staff meetings and not beyond that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One follow-up to exactly that topic. Earlier you said, that can be found on page 79, line 12, you said, during the Crisis Staff meetings there was no mention of mass movement out of town. Then you said: "Another matter are the wishes of certain officials." What kind of "certain officials" are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was to the Prosecutor's question. He mentioned wishes of officials and I said that I could not influence that. And who had what kind of wishes, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, your answer was different. You said: "Another matter are the wishes of certain officials, but I'm not going into that." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that I don't know which official wanted what out of these officials in Sanski Most. At the Crisis Staff, they did not express their wishes, and we did not come to that topic, to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. We would like to see you back after the break, Witness. The break will take 20 minutes. Mr. Lukic, you are still confident that you will be able to conclude today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that I will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take that break. You may follow the usher. And we resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, my attention was drawn to a small issue as far as translation is concerned. And I -- if I could guide the parties to page 74 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 21. And 72, line 22. I wanted to draw your attention as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good, Mr. Lukic. Now, I have only one source, but page 74, line 10, reads now: "Well, I've already said we didn't use that kind of weapon so much there because the resistance in that part of the neighbourhood was less." And I'm informed that the interpreters consider that it should be corrected and that it should now read: "Well, I've already said they didn't use that kind of weapon so much there because the resistance in that part of the neighbourhood was less." That's hereby put on the record. Mr. Lukic, the other thing, you said line 72 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it's correctly recorded four or five houses were hit by those launchers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say it goes almost without saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 72, line 22, it was said "two or three houses only," but actually at that time witness also said "four or five."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That should be verified then by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Definitely, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we could have verified -- because earlier at least we received on the record two to three; whereas, later, indeed, he said four to five, and we'll have to verify that on the basis of the audio. That will be done. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good day.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were speaking about opening fire, mortar fire, at Mahala. Do you know today how many shells were fired and where they fell? Do you know that today or not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know for sure what the locations were, where they fell. They fell between houses or houses that were under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Not more than ten or so shells were fired from a 60-millimetre mortar. It's a small calibre and it doesn't cover a lot of space.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to take a look at two documents only that were shown to you towards the end today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First let us look at P7015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you really asking for P7015 or P7115? That was used during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have here 7015. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Well, that was my mistake. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the document I need. And my colleague showed to the witness page 19 in English and page 3-0 in B/C/S, 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's perhaps the other way around. In B/C/S, it's 19 and English it's 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's the page in B/C/S, at least for now, I need. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2, it says: "The most efficient and most peaceful solution to" ethnic "strife is the transfer of peoples from one area to another." You've already told us that in July 1992 you were not in Sanski Most. In relation to this, I would like to show you document 7116 in order to be able to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's P number, yes, Your Honour. Sorry. P7116.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are minutes again from a session of the Executive Committee, and you told us that you were not even a member of that body. And the date here is the 27th of July, 1992. My colleague read out a portion to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in English, and page 5 in B/C/S. [In English] I have good page in B/C/S, but in e-court I found this on page 6. Can we go back, since we need item 4, and on our screens we have items 7, 8, and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Item 4 is on page 3 in e-court -- no, that's apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Page 3 of the English is item 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 3 in e-court in English. That's where I've item 4. Yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last line in the English version, and line 5 of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- where Vlado Vrkes is speaking in B/C/S, and it says that: "The most humane thing is to allow them to move away peacefully. Certain results have been achieved, efforts are being made through UNPROFOR to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the next page in English, sorry. I'll read again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "... efforts are being made through UNPROFOR to resettle people who are interested in leaving the territory of our municipality." When you attended Crisis Staff sessions, was there any discussion at all about the departure of civilians from the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, there were discussions about civilians who had expressed the wish to leave Sanski Most; ethnic Croats and Muslims, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. That is all I had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question to exactly that portion you discussed with the witness, Mr. Lukic. If you look at the next sentence, which reads as follows, I quote: "We have to persist in this work because this is what the soldiers and the people of Sanski Most require of us because this has to be a Serbian town." In light of all the questions put to you in that respect, what is your comment on that, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My personal comment, I mean, was that it was necessary to save human lives, even at the expense of having people moved out from a certain area if it has to do with saving human lives, if that is what Vlado Vrkes is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But he is saying that it has to be a Serbian town. Isn't that the reason for moving out Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, he says, and that was probably the reason, and that is his remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've also one question for you. You explained to us that, although you said it was just individuals, but that at least it was read to you that seven lads were involved in arming their, as you said, their families and their neighbours, et cetera. At the same time, you were involved in disarming the Muslims. Now, what's the -- what's the explanation as to why it was in that document even applauded that Serbs were to be armed, and that is what happened, and that Muslims should be disarmed? What is the distinction between the two as far as having the right to be armed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, there were too many armed people on both sides. The more weapons there are, the more probable a larger scale conflict is. So when the Serb authorities took over, then they probably made a decision to disarm the armed population, the Muslim and Croat parts, and in the 6th Sana Brigade, all the soldiers were ethnic Serbs. I mean, it wasn't the Serb people that could be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why could the Serb people not be disarmed? Serb civilians having weapons, and you told us that they were distributed among them. Why would it be only the Muslims and the Croats that should be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the decision, probably, of the SDS and the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I've a question which is a bit in a different area. You told us that those who were loyal to the Serbian republic constitution, they could keep their jobs. Why was it that you only could keep your job if you were in support of that constitution and the new structure of power?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, if a new state was established with a new leadership, and they required the loyalty of these people, it's a demand from the top echelons of those authorities who can remain in their positions and who cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just a matter of who is in power, and if you don't -- if you are not loyal to them, you lose your job. Is that -- was that the system?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, probably if that was the demand. Loyalty was required in order to assume a senior position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What justified the Serbs to be in power in Sanski Most? On what basis, apart from force, did they think that they were in power and to require loyalty from non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the same in the other towns and cities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If the Muslims took over power somewhere, their people were in all the senior positions. Whenever the authorities were Croat, the representatives of their ethnic community occupied the majority of senior positions. The Serbs did the same as the other two ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not talking about senior positions. I'm talking about being allowed to stay in the municipality and to keep your job at whatever level.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, if loyalty is required in the management system, it's probably they who decide who can stay in that area and who can keep their jobs if they are qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what you said in your statement. You didn't say the management system would further consider whether someone could stay or not. You said those who were loyal, they could stay and they could keep their jobs. That's what we find in your statement.

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The loyal people remained in their jobs. Those who were loyal to the administration, to the powers, remained in senior positions. In executive positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I'm not talking about executive positions only. And what about being allowed to remain in the municipality? If you were not loyal, was that a valid reason to say that someone should leave?

utterances.speaker: VINKO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think the thinking was that if somebody was an extremist and had taken part in the arming of their people was not loyal and should not be allowed to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to this. No further questions triggered by the questions by the Bench. Mr. Nikolic, I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties or put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put on the record the -- that the Chamber has checked what happened on the 27th of January. In the list of exhibits to be used with this witness, the list of concordance is not included. So just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can agree with Your Honour. That's what I checked and that's what I -- my Case Manager told me that, by mistake, he sent the wrong one. I apologise. And we will make new list of concordance, but maybe we should consult with the staff from your Chamber how that should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most important is that it is done. That's the first of all. And then further details, of course, it's always -- Chamber staff is always open to engage in whatever practical conversations with either party. So if you have good ideas, Mr. Lukic, or if you would develop them over the weekend --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot vouch for that, that they are good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it should be your ambition. But the Chamber staff is always available to further discuss. I'd certainly not exclude the Prosecution in that respect. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, we can also check. And I just would note that, as Your Honours noted, some of the adjudicated facts in the statement are not adjudicated facts of the Mladic trial. So, in that sense, perhaps the statement should also be redacted with respect to some of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If necessary, we'll do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then we'll try to admit the same statement under A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's all fine, Mr. Lukic. But, of course, I take it that you're aware that if you are -- I'm not personally addressing you, but if the Defence is so sloppy in this respect, they, of course, they are at risk if they introduce comments on adjudicated facts who do not even appear, and if I'm able and if we are able to find that out, that in one or two or three minutes, because we didn't have the material any earlier, and it's just a matter of use your computers, find out, check, check, and double-check, and it creates a risk for the -- for the evidence which is presented by the Defence. And the Chamber, at all costs, wants to avoid such risks because we want to pay proper attention to the evidence presented by whatever party. I leave it to that. Some thoughts for over the weekend perhaps. We adjourn for the day and will resume Monday, the 9th of February, 2015, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
